doc.title: Norris Turney interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: A tough life, advice to students and race in studios
summary: Music is a hard living so he tells students to get a degree; black musicians were largely shut out of studio and Broadway work in the 1940s.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Has there been a dark side to the music business for you or any people you know, that we don’t hear about as much? Is it a tough life in some regards?

Oh yeah, it’s a very tough life. A very tough life. Whenever I teach I tell my students, don’t depend on music to make a living by. Go to school and get a degree. Because you can’t make it on music, unless you’re going into rock & roll or something like that.
The music of the 40s, the popular music was swing, so that you could make a living at that time I guess.
Oh yes. You’d go from band to band.
Was there much room in the studio scene for black musicians let’s say during the 40s?

No. Not even on Broadway or in the studios. There were maybe two or three token guys who made all the studio gigs. As a matter of fact I never even thought about that. And there was a lot of things I didn’t know about, the union, I didn’t know about the pension, I didn’t know about the hospitalization. I just happened to look up on it.

Well the musician union was certainly a huge part of music back then. I don’t know if it’s as strong nowadays. If you were in it back then I guess it may pay some dividends for you. And you probably have to do a fair amount of traveling these days to work?
